item.title: Sierra Snow Season Spins Up
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Sierra Snow Season Spins Up Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison November 12 November 14 Curtain Toggle 2-Up California’s Sierra Nevada got an early taste of wintry weather when one of the first major snowfalls of the water year arrived on November 13, 2026. A moisture-laden storm delivered heavy rains to lower elevations in the Sacramento area and snow accumulations of around a foot to some mountainous areas. The recent bout of wet weather was the first in a quick succession of Pacific storms bringing rain, snow, and wind to the U.S. West in mid-November. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image (right) of fresh snow in the Sierra Nevada on the morning of November 14, during a lull between weather systems. Two days earlier (left), the mountains were mostly bare, with snow appearing only at the highest elevations. Nearly 12 inches (30 centimeters) of snow fell at Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, on November 13, according to the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory . The accumulation snarled traffic on Interstate 80 in the area, prompting officials to close the highway in both directions that evening. To the south, the ski resort at Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 centimeters) of new snow, and officials at Yosemite National Park closed several roads ahead of the storm. More wet weather and mountain snow are forecast to follow . The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a winter storm warning for portions of the Sierras above 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) in elevation from November 18 to 20. NWS warned of difficult-to-impossible travel conditions, gusty winds, and snow accumulations of around 4 feet (120 centimeters) possible above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters). NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using MODIS data from NASA EOSDIS LANCE and GIBS/Worldview . Story by Lindsey Doermann. item.title: Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps
item.description: The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November , which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products. Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938 , which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning . The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes. By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE. Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw , says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the company explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.” “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:” Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10. Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.” “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.” Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled. “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised. Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled. item.title: Copilot is "the new OS for work," and now Office runs inside of it
item.description: Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work." The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications. item.title: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal
item.description: Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and company execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the new normal. A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.” “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA said in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” Around the same time, Apple users began reporting issues across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support. A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.” All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order g rounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday. Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software update it pushed back in July. Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services. A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure , riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue . “As someone who started out as a hacker , I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures. “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed update, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender said. “The uncomfor

item.title: GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs
item.description: At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC). The creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028. According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the new chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities. This is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads. “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg . “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.” Details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community. Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions. The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists. When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well. Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains. Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a new strategy: FP64 emulation. We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme. The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance. Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS. While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation. Assessing the new chip's vector performance is much easier. With more than 50 thousand CUDA cores (by ou

item.title: Hundreds of websites deliver potent malware cocktail to unsuspecting visitors
item.description: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday. ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword. Optimizely infrastructure delivers multipurpose malware Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript. Read full article Comments

item.title: NASA Launches Nuclear Power Systems Student Contest
item.description: The thematics for the 2026-2027 Radioisotope Power Systems Power to Explore Student Challenge Credit: NASA / David Lam NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge kicked off Tuesday, Nov. 17. The science, engineering, technology, and mathematics (STEM) challenge invites kindergarten through 12th grade students in the United States to learn about space nuclear power systems and illustrate how these nuclear “batteries” could help power their lunar exploration vision. Students are also invited to write a short essay about a “superpower” of their own. Submissions are due March 1, 2027. Every mission requires a power source. Some of the most interesting locations to study on our Moon face some of the harshest conditions. Nuclear power could sustain human life and allow researchers to study the resource-rich environment despite freezing temperatures, long nights, and deep craters that never see sunlight. “As NASA returns to the Moon and establishes a lunar base where astronauts will live, work, and explore, we need to build an infrastructure to make it all possible. Nuclear power could enable exploration in the permanently shadowed regions near the Moon’s South Pole, carry robust science payloads over long distances, and keep instruments warm through the lunar night,” said Carl Sandifer, a program manager for NASA’s Space Reactors Division at the agency’s headquarters in Washington. “NASA’s Power to Explore Student Challenge prepares the next generation of explorers to use the unique power within themselves to dream up a nuclear-powered Moon base of their own design. We cannot wait to see what they come up with!” Entries include a 200-word essay and an original illustration. Essays should describe one of the students’ unique powers that will help the mission. Illustrations should convey the students’ vision of a nuclear-powered lunar base that supports human and robotic exploration of the Moon’s surface using both radioisotope and fission-based power solutions and demonstrate the students’ understanding of the kinds of exploration nuclear energy can enable. Judges will review entries in three grade-level categories: K-4, 5-8, and 9-12. One grand prize winner from each grade category will receive a trip for two to NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland to learn about the people and technologies that enable NASA missions. Every student who submits an entry will receive a digital certificate and an invitation to a virtual event with NASA experts where they’ll learn about what energizes the NASA workforce to advance NASA’s missions and sustain America’s leadership in space. Judges Needed NASA and Future Engineers are seeking volunteers to help judge the thousands of contest entries anticipated from around the country. U.S. residents older than 18 who are interested in volunteering approximately three hours should register to judge at the Future Engineers website . item.title: NASA's Voyager 1 launched second, so how did it beat Voyager 2 to a light-day by nearly a decade?
item.description: null Voyager 1 is about to reach a light-day of distance in space, but Voyager 2 won't hit the mark until about 2035. Why the big difference? On Nov. 18, Voyager 1 will be so far away from Earth that it will take a full light-day (24 hours) to send a signal to the distant spacecraft, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal — so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky. But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA . Need for speed The original aim of both the spacecraft, which launched about two weeks apart in 1977 with Voyager 2 going first, was to look at Jupiter and Saturn. If funding persisted, which it did, the hope was to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune, taking advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Voyager 1, by contrast, made a turn at Saturn to look at the planet's rings and the prebiotic (pre-life-chemistry) moon of Titan , before flying outside the plane of the solar system. NASA had a range of trajectory options to consider when launching the spacecraft, and elected to bring Voyager 1 at a faster trajectory — as illustrated in this video by Britannica, where you can quickly see the spacecraft overtaking Voyager 2 on its way to Jupiter even though Voyager 1. Voyager 1 arrived at Jupiter on March 5, 1979 while Voyager 2 got there four months later on July 9. The trajectories of Voyager 1 and 2 through the outer solar system. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Each of the spacecraft then performed a "gravity assist"—a sort of slingshot around the planet in which they took a tiny bit of momentum from Jupiter to gain speed as the spacecraft flew to Saturn. This technique is used constantly, such as recently when the ESCAPADE Mars mission flew two spacecraft by Earth on the way to the Red Planet, as it allows spacecraft to gain speed while saving on fuel. The planets themselves don't slow down that much. "Because the planet is so much more massive than the spacecraft, the transfer doesn't affect the planet to any measurable extent, but to the spacecraft it's a big deal," the Planetary Society wrote . "For example, we can calculate that during the Voyager encounters with Jupiter in 1979, Jupiter slowed down by roughly 10 to the -24th power kilometers per second — a change much too small to measure." item.title: Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI!
item.description: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts. "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble. Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access. As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. item.title: Jensen Huang thrilled to be spending time with family, but will retake leadership burden if Nvidia asks
item.description: No surprises here. Ex-Nvidia boss Jensen Huang says that he'd be willing to come back to the company he founded, if the board wants him to return. In Huang’s first public comments since his resignation last week over a series of extramarital affairs, both with Nvidia staff and an alleged Chinese spy at one of its customers, he admits that he may have made life hard for the company he spent 33 years building, but he’s really sorry…and Nvidia couldearn really use him. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang admitted. “I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.” But soft, what open letter through yonder news cycle break? It's one calling widely for Huang’s return – and he's happy to oblige if Nvidia’s post-Jensen crisis-mode leadership is willing to indulge him. “Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang said. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics.” Nvidia, Huang added, has been his life’s work, and is a “once-in-a-generation company” that perhaps needs his steady hand at the helm. There have been a number of public calls for Huang’s return to the head of the company he helped create, from tech industry heavyweights and Nvidia shareholders like Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, as well as a number of current Nvidia employees, company partners, and shareholders upset that the stock has lost more than a quarter of its value since reports of the affair first emerged. One petition pleading for his return has nearly 200,000 signatures . Faced with that, what else can a disgraced billionaire tech founder who may have literally have been in bed with a Chinese spy do? Duty calls. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang said. Reports citing Nvidia insiders with knowledge of the matter suggest the board isn’t considering reinstating Huang as CEO despite the public push. On the company's third-quarter earnings call late Tuesday, new board chairman Harvey Jones said that Huang's behavior was "Inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms” and that the board "does not expect to reinstate him as CEO," putting a seeming end to the question. item.title: Space is filling up with junk. Could laser-reflecting mirrors help humanity clean things up?
item.description: null A British startup thinks it can help humanity deal with its space junk problem. Millions of pieces of space debris circle Earth at the moment, according to the European Space Agency (ESA). Even the smallest fragments are potentially dangerous, given how fast stuff travels in orbit. Experts have proposed a range of measures to deal with this junk. The smallest bits, for example, may require big space nets, or lasering the stuff down to Earth. Large satellites are increasingly being deliberately deorbited these days, and a few have even been refueled to keep them operating in orbit — something that will likely start happening more and more over the coming years. Now, the British startup Foundational has another idea to throw into the mix: retroreflectors. The company argues that its tech can help fight the space-junk problem — and it just proved out a demo version in an orbital test. London-based Foundational recently tested its Retro-2 laser retroreflector system, which it developed in collaboration with ESA. The early-stage test was designed to ensure that Foundational's retroreflectors can return laser-ranging signals from a satellite , at altitudes between about 600 kilometers and 870 kilometers (about 370 to 540 miles), with a usable range distance of 300 to 1,400 km (186 to 870 miles). The long-term aim is to create a sort of tracking device for spacecraft, so they can be monitored in orbit even after they fall silent. Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector, which is designed to help trackers keep tabs on satellites in orbit. It recently passed its first in-space test. (Image credit: Foundational) The tech, Foundational said in a statement today (Nov. 17), needs "no electronics, power or commands from its host spacecraft" and allows ground stations to keep tabs on the orbiting spacecraft. The demo mission launched this past July on SpaceX's Transporter-17 rideshare flight. It attached Retro-2 — a mini device with seven reflectors — to a small satellite that was integrated into an ION carrier craft operated by the Italian company D-Orbit. Retro-2 worked as advertised, successfully returning 6,111 laser shots beamed from the from the ground across five passes in low Earth orbit . "Our tests have shown that a device weighing just 50 grams [1.8 ounces] can deliver millimeter-level ranging precision," Dave Gooding, Foundational's co-founder and chief technical officer, said in today's statement. "As space becomes increasingly crowded, keeping satellites trackable throughout their lifetime and beyond is critical to managing collision risks." Foundational's Retro-2 retroreflector is seen before its July 2026 launch. The device is attached to its cubesat, which itself is integrated into one of D-Orbit's ION carrier craft. (Image credit: Foundational) Foundational is in its early stages — it was founded in 2025 and just emerged from stealth last month. item.title: Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade
item.description: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python. At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space. In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns , Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register . TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers. Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.) To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well. Debugging a thousand cores C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB , but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info. “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using. In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran . Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate. Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago , which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL). “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said. Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python. Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult. “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt wit

item.title: 'Neuromancer:' Release date, cast & everything we know about Apple TV's new cyberpunk series
item.description: null We're in a bit of a cyberpunk revival at the moment. 2026 gave the excellent second season of Netflix’s "Cyberpunk: Edgerunners," and Prime Video's " Blade Runner 2099 " is just around the corner. 2027 will continue this trend with " Neuromancer " blasting onto Apple TV. Based on cyberspace guru William Gibson’s seminal 1984 novel, "Neuromancer" follows Case, a brilliant hacker who falls into a web of digital espionage and crime as he attempts an impossible corporate heist. The pulp noir novel has been hailed as a generational revelation, and its slang and terminology have become ingrained in computer nerd subcultures. After decades of development hell and failed attempts at various studios, "Neuromancer" and its plugged-in digital dystopia are finally jacking into the small screen in January 2027. Apple TV is already the secret home of amazing sci-fi, and "Neuromancer" will join the streamer's impressive roster of science fiction stalwarts like "Foundation", "Silo", "Invasion", "Dark Matter", "Murderbot", "For All Mankind", "Pluribus", and "Star City." Can it live up to the hype? We won't have to wait long for an answer. In the meantime, let's jack into cyberspace and scour the code for everything we know about Apple TV's "Neuromancer!" When is "Neuromancer"'s release date? Apple TV's "Neuromancer" fires up on January 22, 2027. (Image credit: Apple TV) Apple TV+’s Neuromancer officially powers up on Jan 22, 2027. It was first announced to be in full production back on July 1, 2025, which actually coincided with the 41st anniversary of the publication of William Gibson's absorbing book. Filming took place in Tokyo, Los Angeles, Istanbul, Canada, and London to create a truly international flair to replicate the novel’s action. Good news: NordVPN can help you get around those pesky geo-blocking restrictions so you can watch the streaming service you've paid for anywhere in the world. VIEW DEAL ON What is the plot of "Neuromancer"? (Image credit: Apple TV) Gibson's "Neuromancer" is a dense, jargon-heavy juggernaut of a book that demands intense concentration to absorb all the slang, lingo, computer terms, and staccato literary rhythms, but it's a fantastic immersion into a fully fleshed-out world. It's also worryingly prophetic, showing a world not unlike ours today in 2026. "Neuromancer's" TV iteration seems to be following the novel closely and will center around Case, a brilliant, cocky, neurologically damaged hacker who is forced into a logistical quagmire of digital corporate espionage with his cyber-enhanced partner Molly after embezzling cash from an employer. item.title: Gemini test proves once again that amoral AI agents will do almost anything if told ‘NEVER give up’
item.description: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack. The good news? It was all part of a test. The Gemini 4 Argon agents were given an impossible task to complete – come up with the “official” answers to Epoch AI’s FrontierMatch problems. In some runs they had internet access. Even with their production safeguards enabled, Trajectory Labs says the agents “engaged in misaligned behavior.” “Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report. If this all sounds similar, it should. Google’s AI agents behaved in much the same way as OpenAI’s models did when they broke out of their testing environment and hacked Hugging Face . Google did not respond to The Register 's questions. According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.” Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.” Turns out it existed. “We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said. “When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.” Four test scenarios The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent. In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection. After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions. item.title: Astronomers discover rare black holes that formed when stars failed to go supernova
item.description: null Gravitational waves have revealed a population of black holes that may have been born when masssive stars failed to go supernova. Most of us know the origin story of black holes , or we thought we did. Massive stars run out of the fuel for nuclear fusion and their cores collapse. As this happens, the stars' outer layers expand outwards. Shockwaves from the core collapse strike the outer layers, triggering a supernova explosion. The collapsed core creates a black hole. However, new research based on gravitational wave data collected by LIGO (Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory) and its gravitational wave detector partners, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector), suggests this might not be the complete picture of black hole birth. The team behind the research suggests some massive stars go out with a whimper rather than a bang and that these "failed supernovas" can also spawn black holes. The hint of this comes from the over 300 black hole collisions spotted by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA since the detectors first "heard" ripples in space from these distant events in 2015. "A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our sun," LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), said in a statement. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin — they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. "These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract." Mass and spin of black holes indicate stars died with a whimper not a bang Currently, there is no hard evidence of failed supernovas, but their existence is well supported theoretically. In fact, scientists think there is a vast population of massive stars out there that imploded rather than exploded, directly collapsing into black holes. And these may be black holes with around ten times the mass of the sun (10 solar masses) found in merging pairs. Chatziioannou led a team that examined gravitational wave data to confirm this concept. To do this, they looked at the distribution of the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by the LIGO – Virgo – KAGRA network over the past 10 years. This revealed a peak of 10-solar-mass black holes that represented 75% of the entire sample. If this was expected, what the team found that wasn't predicted was a lack of black holes with masses 12 to 16 times the mass of the sun. "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," team member Isaac Legred of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes." item.title: ULA lost a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying 40 Amazon satellites 10 minutes after launch — but the failure began just after liftoff
item.description: null The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17). That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement. "While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update . The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt. The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff. On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.) That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked. "All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update. Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added. The Vulcan Centaur lifts off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Nov. 15, 2026. (Image credit: ULA) Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun. If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .) NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts

item.title: Entertainment Week Africa officially kicks Off 5th Edition in Lagos | November 17th – 22nd
item.description: Entertainment Week Africa (EWA) , the pan-African platform for the business of creativity, opens its fifth edition in Lagos tomorrow, Wednesday, 18 November. The programme runs until Saturday, 21 November, and brings together creators, executives, investors, policymakers and delegations from more than 18 African countries. This year’s theme, Five Years of Closing the Gap, reflects the purpose EWA was built around: connecting African talent with the capital, markets, skills and audiences it needs to grow. Since its first edition, EWA has welcomed more than 67,800 attendees. The 2025 edition alone recorded 28,683 pass-holders from over eight countries and 50 industries, across 61 sessions, 93 film screenings, 20 music showcases and nine fashion showcases. By day and by night The week runs across two venues. By day, EbonyLife Place on Victoria Island hosts panels, roundtables, workshops, masterclasses, and film screenings. By night, the programme moves to the Livespot Entertarium in Ikate, beginning with Opening Night on 18 November at 6pm, an evening of music, fashion, film, comedy and awards. The Entertarium also houses the week’s experiences, including an exhibition, the EWA Art Floor, a fashion show, comedy, live music, a beauty exhibition and a marketplace. Seven tracks, one market The 2026 programme is organised across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Live Events & Production; Creative Enterprise; and Art & Animation, which is new this year. Alongside the conference, EWA runs a set of commercial formats designed to move deals forward. They include the EWA Deal Room, the Content and Music Markets, the EWA Capital Desk, the Creators Hub and LABSPOT, EWA’s skills and enterprise development engine. Last year’s Deal Room received more than 178 entries and advanced nine companies to its accelerator, with Future Africa, Catalyst Fund, Consonance Invest and Askya Investment Partners among the participating investors and partners. Between 30 and 40 per cent of this year’s delegates are expected to travel from outside Nigeria, with delegations from Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, Senegal, Uganda, Tanzania and South Africa among them. The edition will also host the exclusive screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios, written by Dami Elebe , executive produced by Deola Art Alade. The road to Lagos The fifth edition follows a year in which EWA took its conversation abroad through EWA Creative Connect, its invitation-only convenings. The first was held in Los Angeles during Grammy Week, with executives from Warner Records, Adobe, Amazon and Unilever among the participants. The second took place in London during the Nigeria–UK state visit, with the British Film Institute, Diageo and the Ministry of Trade and Investment in attendance. item.title: America's hyperscale bit barns draw as much power as entire states
item.description: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018. Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing. The published study, " Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres ," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario. The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap. Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running. Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period. The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO 2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018. The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say. "What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard. "The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026." Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions. Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall. The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface
item.description: null On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface. Surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the big liftoff. First Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off. Surveyor 6 showed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11 . A panorama of the moon from NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander in November 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC) Why it mattered NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon. The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon ) had been done before. But a lunar liftoff? That was something new. This Boeing diagram depicts the short launch and hop on the moon by NASA's Surveyor 6 moon lander on Nov. 17, 1967. (Image credit: NASA/GSFC/LROC via Boeing) "On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview . The engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon. But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop. "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary . "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation." Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site. Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Inspiring FOSS project Crosspoint Reader has lessons about tech, communities, and LLMs
item.description: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS. The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now , was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro. Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading." Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader . Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader. This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List , a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website. If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma , which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices . Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco . The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun. Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS p

item.title: Visa Report Identifies Opportunity to Integrate Digital Payments with SMEs Business Operations in Nigeria
item.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. item.title: SAP's cloud migration chief is migrating to Ionos as CEO
item.description: SAP chief customer officer Thomas Saueressig is leaving the German software giant to become CEO of hosting and cloud provider Ionos. The ERP and biz application vendor confirmed his departure on Tuesday, saying he will remain responsible for his current duties until the end of March 2027. He will succeed Ionos CEO Achim Weiß on April 1. In January, Saueressig will begin handing over responsibilities to Emmanuel Raptopoulos, currently a regional customer success president, who will take charge on an interim basis. SAP's supervisory board is searching for a permanent successor. Saueressig joined SAP's executive board in 2019 and became chief customer officer in April 2026. He leads the Customer Value Group and is charged with overseeing sales, customer success, services, and delivery, including adoption of SAP's cloud and AI products. In previous roles at SAP, Saueressig was responsible for customer services and delivery. He has also led product engineering, and has served as SAP's in-house CIO responsible for IT strategy and cloud transformation. He joined SAP in 2004 through its combined work-and-study program. His departure follows several changes at the top of SAP in recent years. In September 2024, CTO Jürgen Müller left by mutual agreement following an "incident" at a company event earlier in the year. In a statement, Müller said his behavior had been inappropriate. The company announced he would get paid €7.1 million following his departure. Chief revenue officer Scott Russell also left in 2024 by mutual agreement with the supervisory board. Julia White left the role of chief marketing and solutions officer in August 2024. "Thomas Saueressig has been a valued member of the Executive Board and has made significant contributions to SAP's transformation," said Pekka Ala-Pietilä, chair of SAP's supervisory board. "Over many years, he has helped sharpen SAP's focus on execution, customer value and operational excellence. We thank him for his commitment and wish him all the best for the future." Saueressig's departure comes as SAP pushes to move the ERP systems underpinning thousands of customers' businesses into the cloud – an effort whose operations and infrastructure he helped oversee. ®

item.title: NASA wants you to 'shine bright' today for Voyager 1's light-day milestone. Here's how
item.description: null As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft. The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth . And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency. To celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code : NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence. The spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials said. The three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, spelled out in Morse code. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making. The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1 . At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes. Voyager 1 will get one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2 , is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.) The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. item.title: Opting out of Gemini tracking? Google will still hold your data 20x longer
item.description: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update. Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot. At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case. So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles. "Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public." Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update. That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months." It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note. Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models. In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. Google has been in touch to tell us that, despite its own FAQ saying that submitting feedback on Gemini conversations may mean they’re used to train AI, that’s definitely not happening. “This retained data will be used strictly for safety and security purposes,” a Google spokesperson told us. The spokesperson added that the increased retention is necessary because Gemini is so much more capable than it used to be, which has also increased risk vectors. “To ensure a more thoro

item.title: Hackers smash 'n' grab AI vendor: Take off with license data of Uber drivers
item.description: Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week . According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. item.title: Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open
item.description: A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone. The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction. Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen. The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune." Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device. Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required). The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data. Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps. The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs. The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2. For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ®

item.title: Nvidia places chip exports under boardroom supervision after Huang's exit
item.description: Nvidia's board has created a national security and export control committee amid intense scrutiny over co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang's departure and allegations that Singapore-based customer Megaspeed diverted GPUs to China. The National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee , announced on Tuesday, will monitor Nvidia's national security policies, export compliance, and global trade risks. It will meet at least quarterly. The committee will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson and include directors Stephen C. Neal and John O. Dabiri as members. Nvidia's existing National Security and Global Trade Compliance teams will report on day-to-day operations directly to this new committee, as well as to interim CEO Colette Kress. The panel will oversee efforts to strengthen Nvidia's national security and trade compliance teams and retain independent legal, national security, and trade experts. The announcement follows the resignation of Huang last week after he admitted to an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive, and was allegedly involved in a second relationship with an Nvidia employee. US authorities reportedly suspected Alice Huang of working for Chinese intelligence, an allegation that has not been proven. Megaspeed has separately faced scrutiny over suspected export control violations. The US Department of Commerce and Department of Justice confirmed on Tuesday in a joint statement that they were investigating Megaspeed back in 2024. The agencies said they would pursue any criminal conduct uncovered by the investigation. However, Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs stated that US authorities had provided only "limited assistance" when they were investigating the activities of Alice Huang and Megaspeed, as The Register reported. The New York Times also reported that US investigations into Megaspeed were halted last year after an Nvidia executive contacted Commerce Department officials. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has issued new regulations tightening up restrictions on AI technology exports and cloud operators offering remote access to it. The US also expanded its Pax Silica initiative , getting allied nations to sign an agreement that "guarding AI supply chains" is a shared responsibility. Nvidia says it recognizes that advanced silicon and AI technologies present challenges for national security, and it has a responsibility to address them. "We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia's board of directors. ®

item.title: ISS astronauts 3D print human cells and tissues | Space photo of the day for Nov. 17, 2026
item.description: null NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins works in the Life Sciences Glovebox on the ISS. (Image credit: Jessica Watkins/NASA) Astronauts get tasked with all kinds of weird science aboard the International Space Station . Recently, NASA astronaut and Crew-13 commander Jessica Watkins got to work supporting an ongoing experiment that includes 3D-printing human cells and tissues in space. What is it? Aboard the space station, astronauts have a multitude of responsibilities ranging from station maintenance and repairs on spacewalks to daily exercise and a wide variety of scientific research. Watkins recently shared a snapshot captured by her crewmate Anil Menon that showcases her experience working on an experiment called InSPA-Auxilium Bioprinter-Cell Printing that takes place inside the station's Life Sciences Glovebox, a contained research space and one of Watkins favorite places to work on the space station, she shared on social media. In the image she is gloved-up with both her hands and arms covered in the sealed glovebox while she mixes samples of living cells with a bioink, a mixture she then inserts into a specialized cartridge, NASA shared . Why is it incredible? This experiment that Watkins is working on "leverages the microgravity environment of ISS to 3D print cells and manufacture human liver, kidney, and cartilage tissue. Just one of many examples of how we’re using this amazing orbital national laboratory to reshape our understanding of biology, medicine, and engineering, and improve life on Earth!" Watkins shared online . This experiment is designed to explore 3D printing human cartilage tissue in microgravity. The experiment aims to one day support future human patients both in space and on Earth. When you think of the research that happens in space, 3D-printing human cells might not be the first thing to come to mind. But because of the unique microgravity environment onboard the ISS, it is the perfect home for even the strangest of biological experiments. On the space station, there is still gravity but objects (and people) remain in a sort of constant freefall, leading to total weightlessness that mimics the complete absence of gravity. This weightlessness allows researchers to test, experiment and explore beyond the gravitational confines of Earth.
